data.title: Crypto, Epstein are Dems top oversight targets next Congress
data.description:
• Key insight: The degree to which oversight presents a risk to banks and other financial firms might hinge on the Senate outcome on Tuesday and the extent to which banks have exposure to either disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein or President Trump's crypto businesses. 
  • Forward look: Regardless of whether Democrats win majorities in the election, banks should expect more scrutiny in the next Congress, particularly for large banks and crypto firms. 

WASHINGTON —  Banks and financial firms will likely face a different congressional oversight environment next year as polling suggests Democrats are poised to take back control of both chambers of Congress. 

Experts say that crypto and the largest banks are the most likely targets of oversight if Democrats retake control, particularly those with exposure to President Donald Trump's cryptocurrency business. 

Democrats are widely expected to win back the House on Tuesday, which would put Rep. Maxine Waters, D-Calif., in line to lead the House Financial Services Committee. She might face some inter-party competition for the gavel, three sources familiar with negotiations say, primarily from Rep. Sean Casten, D-Ill., but Waters' seniority and experience on the committee will likely be enough to win her the gavel, and she can be expected to use it to usher in a more aggressive oversight agenda for banks and financial firms. 

The fate of the Senate is less certain. While experts agree there are several paths to Democrats retaking the upper chamber, there are just as many paths for Republicans to eke out a bare majority, or even a 50-50 split. A Democratic takeover of the Senate would bring an even more consequential shift, with longtime Wall Street critic Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., likely to take the chairmanship of the Senate Banking Committee, and with that power will be able to block any White House nominations for bank regulators, including the Federal Reserve.   

To be sure, the amount of actual legislating that Democrats could do would be limited. President Donald Trump would veto most legislation, and even if Democrats win the Senate, they wouldn't have a filibuster-proof majority, and would need to get some Republican support on anything that would have to pass. 

But Democrats can still do a lot with those committees' gavels, including the power over hearing schedules, the ability to issue subpoenas and control over hearing witness lists. 

Bart Naylor, a financial policy advocate at Public Citizen, said Trump's crypto ventures will be a prime target for Democrats, particularly concerning potential conflicts of interests involving his family and companies affiliated with the administration. Public Citizen has argued that Trump's meme coin and other crypto-related dealings raise legal and constitutional questions under the emoluments clause.

"Public opinion polls show that, while the majority of Republicans think this is probably suspect, they're not sure they think it's a conflict of interest," Naylor said. "Simply further establishing that Trump's crypto grift is a conflict and, in my opinion, a legal violation, I think is important." 

Those inquiries could include subpoenas for Trump and people affiliated with his crypto ventures, Naylor said. 

Democrats, especially Warren, will likely return to scrutinizing large banks, including bringing the chief executives of the largest institutions before congressional committees, and focus on the Trump administration's financial regulation rollback. 

The extent of that scrutiny would depend heavily on the Senate results, said Brian Gardner, chief Washington policy strategist at Stifel. If Democrats win the House but Republicans retain the Senate, oversight of the financial sector would largely fall to Waters and the House Financial Services Committee.

Gardner expects Waters to hold hearings with financial regulators and criticize the administration's changes to banking regulation. She could also bring large-bank CEOs before the committee, although he expects housing to be a significant priority for her.

A housing bill could also create a small opening for some legislative action on community banks, Gardner said. Waters would need Republican support to advance such legislation, and Waters has signaled openness for bills specifically affecting smaller institutions with less than $10 billion in assets. 

A Democratic Senate would create a more challenging environment for the banking industry, Gardner said. Warren would have greater resources and more leverage over the administration as Banking Committee chair, including influence over nominations. She is also more attuned to bank regulatory issues, and would usher in more aggressive scrutiny of large banks, consumer protection and the Trump administration's deregulatory agenda. 

Legislatively, there's also small pockets of opportunity for certain bills to pass, particularly those that fall within a slim range of issues where Warren's camp and Trump agree — notably on credit card interest rates. 

For financial firms, the most immediate consequence of a Democratic takeover may be reputational risk rather than changes to the rules governing their businesses. Gardner said he expects additional investigations into the relationship between financial institutions and Jeffrey Epstein. 

"Democrats smell blood in the water on Epstein," Gardner said. "The practical implications are limited, and they are limited to reputational and headline risk that oversight and investigations can uncover something that is not in the public sphere." 

Crypto firms are also preparing for a more difficult political environment. Mary Cull, chief business officer at Cryptex Finance, said she expects investigations into ethics and potential conflicts involving the White House and cryptocurrency companies. She also said a Democratic Senate could complicate efforts to advance crypto market structure legislation.

Cull said the industry continues to want clearer rules as banks and other mainstream financial institutions adopt blockchain technology. The industry, she said, needs a framework that allows innovation while protecting consumers.

"In this administration, I think that crypto has been the darling," she said. "It's been the thing that the Republicans have been obviously pushing through. Obviously there's going to be backlash no matter what happens because it is Washington." 

Banks should pay attention not just to the immediate oversight agenda, Gardner said, but also to how Democrats define their priorities in the next two years ahead of the presidential election. Hearings and investigations could help establish the policy debates that would shape a future administration, even if they do not produce immediate legislative changes.

"I think the next two years are going to be a lot of posturing about what Democrats would do if they had the White House back," Gardner said.

data.title: Why the FTC and 8 states are suing payments fintech Toast
data.description:
• Key insights: The Federal Trade Commission and eight states are suing Toast, alleging that the restaurant software and payments fintech failed to deliver on its customer support promises, made it difficult to cancel its services and hit restaurants with hidden and unauthorized fees and unwanted add-ons. 
  • What's at stake: Toast in a statement said that it "strongly disagrees" with the FTC's allegations and would "vigorously" defend itself. 

The Federal Trade Commission and eight states, including California, Colorado, Florida, Illinois, Iowa, Nebraska, Oklahoma and Utah, are suing restaurant software fintech Toast

Toast is a vertically integrated fintech that sells point-of-sale hardware, software and payment processing services to small businesses in the restaurant industry. Customers can use its products to manage orders, accept payments and track inventory. It also provides those small businesses with working capital loans. 

The lawsuit alleges that the company violated the FTC Act and the Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act — a 2010 law designed to protect online consumers from deceptive marketing practices, hidden subscription charges and unauthorized data passes — by failing to deliver on its customer support promises, making it difficult to cancel its services, and hitting restaurants with hidden and unauthorized fees and unwanted add-ons. 

"Small businesses are the backbone of communities across the country, and they deserve tools and services that are transparent, reliable and truthful," Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC's bureau of consumer protection said in a statement. "Toast failed to honor a number of its promises and instead imposed hidden fees, unauthorized charges and subscription traps that drained the hard‑earned profits of businesses just trying to serve their customers. These practices are illegal, and the FTC will continue to take aggressive action to ensure a fair, transparent and competitive marketplace." 

The FTC said that Toast customers frequently complain that they have been enrolled in, and charged for, Toast subscription add-ons without their consent, and that Toast failed to provide customers with a simple cancellation process. 

Toast in a statement said that it "strongly disagrees" with the FTC's allegations and would "vigorously" defend itself. 

"In this matter, the FTC is seeking to apply the Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act (ROSCA) — a law Congress passed to address certain online subscription practices — to Toast's commercial agreements with its restaurant customers." Toast said. 

"No court has held that ROSCA applies to negotiated business-to-business agreements, and we don't believe it applies here," the company said. "Such an application has the potential to rewrite the laws of commercial contracts and disrupt business-to-business providers across the economy, ultimately resulting in less competitive terms and more harm to small businesses."

The FTC has been looking into the allegations for more than a year. 

"Toast has been cooperating fully with the FTC's review of this matter since mid-2025 and has engaged in good faith throughout, including efforts to reach a resolution short of litigation," Toast said. "The FTC disregarded the information we provided showing the extent to which our restaurant customers negotiate their contracts.

"We are prepared to defend our business and fight this unprecedented action through litigation." 

ROSCA compliance is an FTC investigation and enforcement priority, and is "aggressively" enforced by the federal regulator and state attorneys general as unfair and deceptive acts or practices, according to Richard Newman, a partner at the law firm Hinch Newman who specializes in advertising and digital media. 

As of December 17, 2025, the FTC has undertaken approximately 50 ROSCA actions, with the largest settlement amounting to $2.5 billion, according to Hinch Newman.

data.title: OCC floats preemption of California climate-disclosure laws
data.description:
• Key insight: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency is suggesting that California's climate-disclosure laws may be preempted by federal banking laws, urging a state regulator to exempt national banks before it moves to formalize that preemption. 
  • Supporting data: California Senate Bill 253 requires firms with $1 billion or more in revenue to quantify and disclose investment-related emissions and another Senate Bill 263 requires climate-risk reports from firms with $500 million or more in revenue.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency on Thursday urged a California environmental regulator to exempt nationally chartered banks from two laws that require firms to measure their lending and investment-related greenhouse gas emissions and disclose climate-related financial risks. 

In the letter to the California Air Resources Board Chair Lauren Sanchez, Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould argued the state's climate disclosure regime is likely to "decrease competition, drive up prices, and reduce Californians' access to financial services" and said the state laws' applicability to national banks may be preempted\. 

"The disclosure laws would be inconsistent with OCC regulation and safety and soundness; impose undue burden, particularly on smaller banks; harm California customers and disrupt customer relationships; and raise constitutional concerns, including under the Supremacy Clause," the OCC announced in a press release. "The application of the laws to banks may well run afoul of the legal framework for preemption and visitation, which are critical components of the dual banking system that Congress created over 150 years ago."

The agency under Comptroller Jonathan Gould has taken an active role in an ongoing legal and regulatory battle over how and to what degree state laws may affect national banks, notably moving to preempt an Illinois' law restricting interchange fees on taxes and tips earlier this year. Experts say the OCC's current expansive preemption stance is likely to end up in the Supreme Court. 

The letter comes in response to Senate Bill 253 and Senate Bill 261, both climate related measures passed in 2023 that direct companies to take steps to address climate-related financial risks. Under Bill 253, companies with more than $1 billion in revenue will need to submit greenhouse gas emissions reports by next month. Bill 261 requires companies with $500 million or more in revenue to draft reports on climate-related financial risks, though that law is currently under a temporary injunction while it is under review by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit. 

The OCC is arguing the requirements unnecessarily draw resources away from material financial risks and took issue with the blunt asset thresholds, which do not consider banks' individual risk profiles.

"As the disclosure laws would apply to federally chartered banks without any assessment of risk to the bank and would require the banks to devote significant resources to comply with the laws, the disclosure laws run directly counter to the OCC's regulation and supervision of federally chartered banks," the letter reads. "As such, it will not advance safety and soundness and, in some cases, could undermine it by distracting bank management. Congress intentionally structured the federal banking system to guard against precisely these kinds of competing demands."

The agency also argued that banks would need to request arduous and exhaustive information from borrowers to meet the disclosure requirements, something customers could view as intrusive. Smaller banks may be particularly likely to end their relationships with California-based customers to avoid the compliance burden, the agency continued. 

Read more:

  • Fed will drop one interest rate vote next year; two in 2028
  • UMB says deal gives it access to wealth fleeing California
  • CFPB flunks cybersecurity audit amid staff cuts: OIG report
  • BofA adds Wisconsin to branch map, with more states to come

"The application of the disclosure laws to federally chartered banks may well run afoul of this legal framework," Gould noted. "The OCC will evaluate CARB's implementation of the disclosure laws to determine whether further action is necessary to provide federally chartered banks with certainty as to the application of the law."

The second Trump administration has been thorough in its effort to cull any climate-related banking regulatory initiatives that had been enacted during the Biden administration, arguing climate is outside the remit of bank regulation. 

Last year, the agency stopped considering the risk of climate events to bank's business models and said it hampered institutions and their regulators and were duplicative of other regulatory requirements. Months earlier, the OCC withdrew from an international body devoted to combatting climate-driven financial risks known as the Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System after similar moves by the Federal Reserve Board and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp.

data.title: The credit market is strained but growing; crypto's historic hack
data.description:
Credible growth
My general working hypothesis about economic growth is that as long as the credit market is expanding, everything else is secondary. Yes, inflation is too high and it's a real burden for lots of people and I get sticker shock every time I'm in a grocery store. The jobs market is marginal and wage growth is not keeping pace. And those things do of course affect the credit market. But until the credit market stops working, it is still growing. I know that sounds obvious, but it's important.

We have a few stories that shed some anecdotal light on the state of the credit market. Newtek, which is the largest Small Business Administration lender in the country, said high interest rates and inflation resulted in a higher level of problem loans in its portfolio, our John Reosti reported. It has been particularly acute for borrowers who took out loans before 2022, the company said, when rates started rising. The company's third-quarter earnings fell 40%. "There's been stress on the historic portfolio," CEO Barry Sloane said.

Meanwhile, the company formerly known as LendingClub, which now calls itself Happen Bank, saw a sharp increase in its earnings as a result of, well, people taking out new loans, our Melinda Lucy reports. Originations, mainly personal and home-improvement loans, rose 26%. "Customers have so much equity in their homes and are sort of stuck," CEO Scott Sanborn said.

It's impossible to draw any conclusion from that except for the fact that the credit market is so big some people are struggling and others aren't. 

The overall problem with credit is that it has a tendency to grow and grow and grow until it becomes a problem, thanks to the miracle known as compounding interest. Former Treasury Secretary Hank Paulson, who was in that job the last time the credit market melted down, warned that the current national debt, which topped $40 trillion a month ago, has become unsustainable. Our Nathan Place tramped over to the Economic Club of New York for the speech.

"If not addressed, it will strangle our economy," Paulson said. 

He  isn't the first to say that, of course. Profligate spending by the federal government has been a concern for decades. The reason it hasn't blown up in our faces is complex, but it can be boiled down to the fact that our creditors overall believe that we're still good for the money, that the world's largest economy can continue to service its debt.

The problem with that is that the debt is now spiraling higher — interest payments are now more than $1 trillion a year — thanks to the miracle known as compounding interest. At some point (and you could make a fortune if you could predict it) our creditors will change their mind about us. 

Binance robbery
People rob banks. Sometimes it's an inside job, sometimes it's a Dillinger-style heist. Usually what they are stealing is cash, because cash is largely untraceable, but cash has its drawbacks, the main one being that you can carry only so much of it. 

You can, though, carry a virtually unlimited amount of digital money on a thumb drive, which makes cryptocurrencies a very lucrative target. Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, acknowledged last night that somebody had stolen about $6 billion worth of cryptocurrencies from its accounts, which reports say is the largest theft in the industry's nearly 20-year history (though the website rekt.news, which tracks crypt thefts, notes a bitcoin miner named Lubian lost $3.5 billion in 2020, which would be worth $14 billion today).

The exchange said it was suspending withdrawals, and deposits for that matter, on its platform and pledged to make its customers whole. I suppose on one level it's kind of impressive that Binance has that kind of money sitting around, but still shutting down its entire platform and draining $6 billion from its reserves is a big expense. By comparison, "London Whale" trade Bruno Iksil cost JPMorgan $6 billion. If Binance was a publicly traded company, fines would be on tap and an executive or two would probably be getting fired. They may anyhow.

Read more:

  • Forget jobs or inflation, credit is what matters. And credit is…
  • For both de novos and prediction markets, it's how you read the law
  • Those sleepy deposits that are 90% of your customers are waking up
  • Crypto and bitcoin have problems the CFTC and SEC can't fix

The reason people steal cryptocurrencies is because most of them are designed to mimic physical cash in that they are digital bearer bonds. If you hold the "keys" to the wallet that contains the money, you hold the money. The stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle froze more than $2 billion worth of the stolen money, because they have designed their systems differently. But that still leaves $4 billion out there beyond reach. It's probably gone.

Dillinger would have loved crypto markets, but these are the issues banks will have to contend with before they really embrace digital money.

data.title: Extortion group leaks keys to bank vendor's Fed firewall
data.description:
• Key insight: An extortion group published not only system keys and credentials but also a map of how Finzly's firewall connects to other systems.
  • What's at stake: Finzly's 11 listed bank and credit union clients share a single connection to ACH, Fedwire and FedNow, and the leaked files describe a direct link to the Fed with rules for FedNow and FedACH traffic.

Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review.

This week, a cyber extortion group, n0n, published the passwords and keys to a firewall that guards the link that Finzly's bank clients use to send payment instructions to the Federal Reserve. The group also published details about how the firewall is set up and how it connects to other systems.

Finzly, a company that connects banks to payment networks, says the leaked files can't get anyone into its systems. The company has "rotated system keys and credentials," a company spokesperson told American Banker.

Regardless of changing the passwords, "the possession of the compromised configuration information alone does not provide access to our systems or data," the spokesperson said.

Federal Reserve payment services "were not impacted," a Fed spokesperson said.

Finzly sells a platform, BankOS, that links banks to ACH, Fedwire, FedNow and other payment networks through a single connection shared by all its clients. Its website listed 11 banks and credit unions as clients last week.

Finzly's investigation so far shows "no evidence that customer data or access information related to our banking customers' systems was compromised," the spokesperson said. "At no point were Finzly's customer operations impacted."

Finzly has notified law enforcement, hired outside legal and forensic experts and begun communicating with customers, the spokesperson said. "We continue to work closely with regulators and our customers," they said.

American Banker reviewed the publicly available files; they do not contain customer data, bank data or transaction records. American Banker did not test whether the leaked keys or passwords work.

Annotations in the files call the configuration the "2023 config," suggesting it dates to that year.

N0n threatened last week to publish "network configuration and access secrets for payment infrastructure" unless Finzly paid. It extended the deadline from Friday to Tuesday night, then it posted the files after the extension passed, suggesting Finzly did not pay.

N0n's listing did not say how much it wanted from Finzly. The group's listings of South Korean companies demanded between $600,000 and $14 million in bitcoin, according to a report from the threat-intelligence firm Cyfirma.

How it went down

It is unclear exactly how n0n obtained the passwords and keys.

The Finzly spokesperson said only that the company determined that "an unauthorized third party accessed a single device in our backup data center containing configuration information."

The statement did not say whether that device was the firewall, when the access happened or how the intruder got in.

Five of the six files n0n posted this week appear to make up the configuration of a Fortinet FortiGate firewall, which is a device that sits between a company's systems and the outside world and controls what traffic passes between them.

The sixth file contains a summary of the configuration and calls the firewall a "payment gateway."

The files describe a direct link labeled "FED" and firewall rules labeled for FedNow and FedACH traffic.

Firewalls normally store passwords and keys in scrambled, encrypted form. The summary file says the ones in this configuration were decrypted on Oct. 15.

Fortinet (like other firewall makers) has protected such secrets with hard-coded or weak encryption keys in the past; Fortinet acknowledged in 2019 that older versions of its firewall software used a single hard-coded key, identical on every device, to encrypt passwords in configuration files.

As such, it is "absolutely plausible" that n0n got the keys by decrypting the configuration, according to Michael Tigges, a principal tactical response analyst at the cybersecurity firm Huntress.

What could have happened

By Finzly's account, the files n0n leaked no longer offer a way into its systems, but the episode could have gone much worse had the group used the passwords and keys to get in.

In the worst case, a leaked firewall configuration "can lead to total domain compromise," or an attacker's control of an entire network, according to Tigges.

It also could have led to the theft of data such as account numbers and financial transactions, and "potentially ransomware," he said.

It is unclear whether n0n tried to use the passwords and keys for any of these purposes before turning to extortion.

It is also unclear whether Finzly detected n0n's access to the keys before the group started extorting the company, or whether it was n0n's extortion that tipped the company off that something was awry.

Finzly has not said when it changed the keys, so it is unclear whether it did so before or after the group obtained or published them.

What changing the keys doesn't fix

An old firewall configuration still holds information about what connections a network trusts, even if the passwords have changed, according to Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat research at Sophos, a security company that also sells firewalls.

In this case, the configuration offers a map of the tunnels to Finzly's cloud systems and its direct link to the Fed. That map can show an attacker which systems talk to which and where to aim on the way to the one it wants to access.

Changing passwords doesn't change those connections, so a map of them still saves an attacker much of the work of scouting a target, Pilling told American Banker.

"Network layouts, IP addresses, tunnel endpoints, and trust relationships change far more slowly than passwords," Waseem Ahmed, head of engineering at the security firm Secure.com, told American Banker.

In other words, Finzly can change the locks on its own systems quickly, but redrawing the map attackers now hold (by changing how the systems connect to each other) would take far longer.

What banks should do

A bank whose vendor's firewall configuration has leaked should first ask the vendor one thing, according to Denis Calderone, chief technology officer at the security firm Suzu Labs: "Have you rotated every credential and key in that file, and can you show me?"

He would also ask whether the vendor told the Fed.

A bank should also list every connection it has to the vendor, change every credential it controls and agree on new VPN keys with the vendor "rather than waiting to be told," Ahmed said.

Finally, banks should check their logs for unusual connections from the vendor's systems "going back months, not just since the leak," Calderone said.

data.title: BankThink The future of AI in banking is not as clear as you might think
data.description:
• Key insight: Even the leaders of the largest banks in the country can't agree on the impact artificial intelligence will have on the industry. But there are some steps everyone can take to ease the transition.
  • Forward look: Leaders should be asking their people what they're seeing, what they're concerned about and where they believe AI might actually help them do their jobs better. The people closest to the work often have the clearest view of both the opportunities and the risks.

I recently had the opportunity to deliver the opening keynote at a national conference for a professional association outside the banking industry. Out of curiosity, I asked the several hundred people in the audience if any of them worked in banking. Maybe 10 hands went up.
I knew that would be the case going in, but I wanted visual confirmation. I smiled as I thought about the hundreds of times over the years that banking leaders have told me that most of my subject matter and some of my more passionate proclamations are not specific to banking.

In this instance, I was asked to speak on two subjects: organizational change management, which I consider an evergreen topic, and the humanization of artificial intelligence, which is quickly becoming one as well.

And, to be honest, helping people understand and adopt AI may be one of the biggest change management challenges of our careers.

I was particularly interested in seeing whether nonbankers would have some of the same reactions to my personal takes on everything from AI adoption to building more unified teams, improving internal communications, and even sales and business development.

Full disclosure: Regardless of the business subject I'm asked to address, I'll always find a way to work "sales is oxygen" into the mix. There are few more objective measures of leadership effectiveness and a company's health than whether the business is growing profitably over time.

When discussing the current state of the AI debate across industries, I shared a true story from earlier this year. While speaking at a large banking conference, I suggested that bank leaders were totally justified in being cautious and even a bit skeptical of some of the bold promises being made about AI.

Two things can be true. AI may eventually change everything. But eventually may take longer than we're being told, and the road may be bumpier than we're being led to believe.

Apparently, when I borrowed the quote, "Don't ask the barber whether you need a haircut," I sent the speaker who followed me into a bit of a tizzy. He literally stepped outside to change some of his slides to address the "AI denier" who kicked off the conference.

When I later sat near that speaker at dinner, I laughed and told him that if he had stayed in the room, he might have had a better understanding of the point I was making.

I gave him an example: Hey, I like fire. I'm a fan of fireplaces and grilling steaks over an open flame. That said, I'm anti forest fires. And for the record, I'm anti arsonist as well.

Until we have a good handle on not setting our house on fire, we need to really watch the stove.

Read more:

  • Banks are blocking external AI agents. Is this sustainable?
  • Even the largest US banks measure AI returns differently
  • Bankers grapple with liability when AI agents mess up
  • Banks should consider Palantir CEO's critique of OpenAI, Anthropic

I was also recently invited to a CEO retreat attended by leaders of many banks, including some of the largest in the country. During his talk, the CEO of a top 10 bank solemnly vowed that his bank would never, ever allow an outside AI agent to have control over an account at his bank.

A little later, an executive from another financial services company took the stage and, in good humor, said, "Yeah … uh … good luck with that."

The room full of bank executives and investors chuckled, but the point was made. For all the tremendous opportunities AI presents to make companies more efficient and responsive, it also creates customer protection challenges few could have imagined just a few years ago.

Therein lies one of the biggest challenges leaders face with AI. If experienced executives can't agree on what the future looks like, imagine what employees are thinking as they try to figure out what it means for their jobs, their customers and their careers.

That's why I've been reminding bank leaders at all levels that there has never been a time when consistent communication with our teams mattered more. Any new programs, policies, and practices involving AI should be clearly and continually explained. So should any restrictions on its use.

And communication needs to be a two-way street. Leaders should be asking their people what they're seeing, what they're concerned about and where they believe AI might actually help them do their jobs better.

The people closest to the work often have the clearest view of both the opportunities and the risks.

Afterward, people from that nonbanking audience came up to tell me they were facing many of the same challenges with AI that I had described.

Technology may change how we do business, but the fundamentals of leading people through change remain remarkably consistent.

Communicate clearly. Listen carefully. And do both often.

data.title: Wearable payments get a boost from new market entrants
data.description:
• Key insight: Wearables are a small part of the payments market, but are growing quickly. 
  • Expert quote: "There are all sorts of things that are increasingly possible." —Celent's Gareth Lodge.

The wearables market is gaining traction, with smartwatches, rings, smart glasses and wristbands poised to gain popularity as payment devices.

A report from the Business Research Company valued the global market for wearable payments at $79.59 billion in 2025. The global market research and consulting firm predicts the market will grow to $94.4 billion in 2026, with expectations to reach $186.25 billion by 2030 at a compound annual growth rate of 18.5%. North America was the largest region for growth last year, with the Asia-Pacific region growing the fastest.

To be sure, use of wearables for payments pales in comparison with credit cards or mobile phones, but that could change over time as AI improves, wearable devices become more readily available, and with sufficient consumer, bank, and merchant education, Gareth Lodge, principal analyst at Celent, told American Banker. "There are all sorts of things that are increasingly possible," he said.

Here's what banks need to know about recent developments in wearable payment devices.

Factors influencing growth

The Business Research Company expects several factors to drive growth, including growing adoption of contactless payments, the ongoing expansion of payment-enabled wearable devices, advancements in secure payment technologies, and expanding use of tokenization and secure authentication.

For instance, DIGISEQ, a wearable payment technology company, announced last year that it was adding Visa tokenization, expanding beyond its existing Mastercard token provisioning for a range of wearable devices, including rings, bracelets, cards and key fobs.

"Although the market faces certain challenges, including the need for alternative authentication methods for screenless devices such as rings, uneven issuer support across countries, and variations in transit acceptance, these constraints are manageable," according to Business Research Company. "Rather than limiting overall market growth, they are likely to influence the pace of adoption and determine which wearable payment form factors achieve wider market penetration first."

Which devices show the most promise

Smartwatches are expected to remain the largest segment through 2030, supported by their established user base, integrated authentication features, and well-developed payment ecosystems, including Apple Pay, Google Wallet, and Samsung Wallet, according to Business Research Company.

Payment opportunities are also emerging within smart rings, which are expected to notch the fastest growth, according to Business Research Company. Circular, for instance, recently announced its new Circular Ring 3 series at IFA, the consumer tech show in Berlin.

Other opportunities exist in payment bands and wristbands and smart glasses, which may also progress from early stage adoption to a more established market segment, with Asia-Pacific potentially leading this development, according to Business Research Company.

AI glasses from several Chinese big tech companies, including Alibaba, have payment functionality, according to a January equity research report from Barclays. Also, Rokid, which specializes in lightweight, AI-powered smart eyewear, recently partnered with Ant International to enable payment functionality on its smart glasses. 

Even so, it's still an up-and-coming product set. "AI glasses remain far from maturity," according to Barclays. "The industry's expansion will be closely tied to continuous improvements in AI functionality and product usability. Users primarily focus on AI features such as AI interaction, translation, and photo/video capture. Also, product usability remains critical, where consumers care about weight, lens display quality, product design, and battery life due to daily usage," Barclays wrote.

The future is unwritten

Product-makers need to consider the potential for widespread adoption, Lodge told American Banker. "Phones can do so many different things already. Whenever something new comes along, it has to be as good or do something better than what's existing."

A lot hinges on consumers' appetite for these products. "As long as you trust the company that's offering it with your personal data, it would be a good growth market for payments," Deb Baxley, partner at payment consultancy PayGility Advisors and member of the U.S. Payments Forum's Steering Committee, told American Banker. "Just adding payments increases the utility of it."

Certainly, other wearable makers could eventually push into the payments space. Amazon, for instance, earlier this month announced the availability of Bee Frontier, its next-generation AI wearable that can be worn on a person's wrist or clipped to clothes. It's equipped with dual microphones with advanced noise filtering, so it can take notes on important meetings, plans, or help users remember to make purchases. 

While the Bee Frontier doesn't have payment capabilities today, some industry watchers suggest it could be on the horizon. Alexa never drove the shopping that Amazon expected it to, but a product like Bee Frontier could, Celent's Lodge told American Banker. Amazon did not respond to a request for comment.

Meta, which last year acquired Limitless, the maker of the Limitless Pendant, is reportedly working on an upgraded AI-powered wearable pendant. Meta did not respond to a request for comment about whether the pendant would be equipped with payment capabilities.

data.title: Credit issues put damper on profits at SBA specialist Newtek
data.description:
• Key takeaway: Newtek CEO Barry Sloane is hopeful that both oil prices and inflation will lessen following the mid-term elections, improving his company's asset-quality profile.
  • Expert quote: "At these higher levels of rates, it is more challenging to make loans, it's more challenging to run the business." — Sloane

The nation's largest Small Business Administration lender by number of loans says higher-for-longer interest rates and stubborn inflation are pushing problem-loan levels higher, while also dampening the company's growth prospects.  

A cocktail of higher rates and inflation "has been difficult" on NewtekOne's entire portfolio, CEO Barry Sloane said Wednesday during a call with analysts.

Conditions have proven particularly challenging for small businesses that obtained their loans prior to 2022, when rates began rising. They've seen inflation crimp profits, even as their borrowing costs have soared. "There's been stress on the historic portfolio," Sloane told analysts.

Boca Raton, Florida-based Newtek reported its third-quarter earnings Wednesday. Net income totaled $10.7 million, down 40% from the same period in 2025. At the same time, nonaccrual loans more than doubled, reaching $383.2 million on Sept. 30.

The spike in problem loans prompted Newtek to more than double its provision for credit losses to $15.4 million for the quarter ended Sept. 30. The company has also tightened underwriting and tamped down on its growth targets.

"At these higher levels of rates, it is more challenging to make loans, it's more challenging to run the business," Sloane said. "Therefore we have muted our origination volumes … and we've also tightened underwriting guidelines historically and are doing so as we speak right now."

Piper Sandler analyst Crispin Love described Newtek's credit picture as "mixed" in a research note Thursday. Love cited the increase in nonaccrual loans, but he also noted that early-stage delinquencies declined from their June 30 level.

Though Newtek has been a prominent SBA lender for more than a decade, it operated for most of that time as a non-depository business development company.

In January 2023, Newtek bought the one-branch National Bank of New York City, intending to use less costly bank deposits to fund loans. Since closing the deal, the $3.5 billion Newtek has grown deposits at the bank, which it renamed Newtek Bank, from $141.6 million to $2.5 billion.

Robust deposit growth and an improved funding profile provided Newtek leeway to scale back the volume of SBA loans it sells to investors on the secondary market, a course it announced it would adopt in August. Interest income has responded, totaling $53.4 million for the quarter ended Sept. 30, increasing 15% on a linked-quarter basis and 36% year-over-year. 

And Newtek is by no means the only SBA lender to report third-quarter credit quality issues. At the $9.9 billion-asset, Chicago-based Byline Bancorp, government-guaranteed nonperforming assets reached $9.7 million on Sept. 30, up 15% year-over-year.

Meanwhile, at the $1.46 billion-asset, Las Vegas-based GBank Financial Holdings, government-guaranteed nonaccrual assets remained elevated, totaling $25.5 million on Sept. 30, their fifth consecutive quarter over $25 million.

"Credit costs have weighed on earnings this year," GBank CEO Jeff Newgard said Wednesday on a conference call with analysts. 

SBA's biggest loan programs, 7(a) and 504, operate by guaranteeing loans made by banks, credit unions and other lenders.

Read more:

  • Fed will drop one interest rate vote next year; two in 2028
  • UMB says deal gives it access to wealth fleeing California
  • CFPB flunks cybersecurity audit amid staff cuts: OIG report
  • BofA adds Wisconsin to branch map, with more states to come

For his part, Sloane remains hopeful a post-election economic upturn will boost Newtek's returns. 

"Once we get through these mid-terms, I think that oil, which has been the primary driver of inflation, will hopefully move in the right direction, reduce rates, reduce inflation and give us a lift," he said.

During SBA's 2026 fiscal year, which ended Sept. 30, Newtek was credited with originating 5,035 7(a) loans, 1,436 more than Portland, Maine-based Northeast Bank, the number-two lender by number of loans. The 7(a) program is SBA's largest loan program. It approved 56,130 loans during fiscal 2026.

data.title: Wells Fargo raises hurdle for higher advisor payouts for first time in 5 years
data.description:
• Key insight: Wells Fargo becomes the latest wirehouse to require advisors to produce a bit more to earn the same take-home pay. In its case, it's raising a monthly revenue-production hurdle they must cross to earn a higher payout rate.
  • Supporting data: Advisors on average will have to increase their revenue production by 2%, or about 2%, or $15,000 a year, to avoid a pay reduction, said Sol Gindi, head of Wells Fargo Advisors.

Wells Fargo is upping the monthly revenue-production hurdle advisors have to cross to gain a pay boost while also requiring them to show asset growth if they want to avoid a cut in their deferred compensation.

Those were two of the biggest changes Wells Fargo announced Thursday to its advisor compensation policies for 2027. Along with various smaller adjustments, Wells said it was raising the monthly amount of revenue advisors must generate to see a bump in their payout rate. Under the current policy, advisors keep 22% of the first $13,500 in monthly revenue generated for the firm and 50% on anything above that. Next year, the hurdle for that payout boost will go up to $16,000.

Wells Fargo Advisors Head Sol Gindi said in an interview Thursday that this is the first time the hurdle has been adjusted in about five years. Since then, Wells Fargo advisors' revenue production has risen by 57% on average, in part buoyed by the strong stock market.

"And we've done a lot in the last five years, right?" Gindi said. "We've invested in the business, we restructured the business, the business is growing. You know, our FAs are larger. Our advisors now have so many more tools to grow and we want to see more of them growing."

At the same time, Wells Fargo is keeping in place "enhanced grid" payouts for advisors who bring in $2 million or more in net new assets over the past 12 months and generate $2 million or more in additional revenue in the same period. Advisors who meet both criteria get to keep 50% of the revenue they generate for the firm.

READ MORE: What to expect in advisor pay in 2026 

Some Wells advisors to get an $8,400-a-year haircut

Andrew Tasnady, a compensation consultant and the founder of Tasnady & Associates, said the hurdle increase will cost advisors $8,400 a year if they don't qualify for the enhanced grid. But Wells Fargo gives advisors plenty of ways to make that up by generating more revenue and earning various rewards and bonuses.

"If you do one $1 million loan, you get 75 basis points on that, and that's $7,500," Tasnady said. "So it's not tragic."

Gindi said advisors on average will have to increase their revenue production by about 2%, or about $15,000 a year, in order to offset any income losses. 

"You know, we've delivered so much more growth than that, and they have more opportunity going forward than that," he said. "So that's how we're thinking about it."

READ MORE: Wells Fargo private wealth head taps firm's full capabilities for clients 

Lowered deferred comp for advisors who aren't growing

In others change intended to encourage growth, Wells Fargo is boosting deferred compensation for advisors who bring in new assets while lowering it for those whose asset totals remain the same or fall. Advisors whose assets are growing will see their deferred payouts rise to a range of 6% to 11% of their current revenue production. That's up from a range of 5% to 10% now.

Meanwhile, advisors whose totals are stagnant or falling will see their deferred payouts reduced to a range of 3% to 8%. Deferred compensation is paid after an interval of several years and is often portrayed as a bonus that rewards advisors for staying with a firm. Wells Fargo advisors make no deferred compensation if they generate $714,000 or less in annual revenue and are paid it at varying rates for revenue above that.

"Advisors who are growing their businesses and deepening relationships and bringing the full capabilities of Wells Fargo to bear, they're going to do the best under the plan," Gindi said. "And I think they're going to do the best anywhere with this plan."

Tasnady noted that Wells Fargo's wirehouse rival Merrill saw an increase in advisor departures when it adopted an unpopular "growth" compensation grid in 2018 that similarly punished advisors for not bringing in more assets. Tasnady said people never like to think money is being taken away from them.

One important distinction for Wells' 2027 policy, he noted, is that its reduced payout will be "on deferred and not the cash payout like Merrill's."

READ MORE: How Wells Fargo keeps advisors by letting them go independent 

A few added sweeteners

Alongside those larger changes, Wells Fargo is also adding various sweeteners to encourage advisors to take actions like help to open banking accounts and arrange loans for clients. For instance, Wells will start offering a reward for opening or moving money into business-checking accounts for clients. Advisors will receive 15 basis points (0.15%) for moving money into a business-checking account without a priority credit line — which is used to arrange security-backed loans — and 25 basis points (0.25%) on money moved into accounts with a PCL. 

Wells Fargo will offer deferred rewards to advisors whose clients move money into deposit accounts, on top of the rewards already provided for arranging lines of credit and providing mortgages and other one-time products. The new reward will be equal to 150% of their year-over-year growth in revenue from checking or other deposits.

Wells Fargo is the last of the four large wirehouse firms to announce its pay policies for 2027. Of the others, Merrill and UBS are keeping their basic payout grids unchanged, while Morgan Stanley adjusted its to require advisors to produce a little bit more revenue to maintain their compensation.

Wells Fargo has consistently had one of the most-generous payout grids among wirehouses. For advisors producing $1 million in annual revenue, it paid $468,965 this year — putting it behind only UBS. For those at the $2 million production level, it was the top payer, offering just over $1 million.

data.title: Mastercard touts the importance of agentic tokens
data.description:
• Key insights: Masercard CEO Michael Miebach said during the company's third quarter earnings call that one-time virtual cards as a go-between between agents and merchants were not a long-term solution to facilitate agentic payments.
  • What's at stake: Visa, Mastercard and American Express have taken the position that tokenization is the best technology to capture consumer intent and maintain trust within agentic commerce transactions. 

Mastercard isn't too keen on using one-time virtual cards to facilitate agentic transactions — at least in the long term. 

CEO Michael Miebach stressed Mastercard's position that tokenization was the best technology to make widespread agentic commerce possible during the company's third quarter earnings call on Thursday. 

An agentic token is similar to other payment tokens used in e-commerce and near-field communication. It substitutes payment credentials for a randomly generated number to authorize a transaction, but it also carries information about what the agent is allowed to do based on predefined rules or permissions, according to VGS, a data security and compliance fintech. 

"It is in everybody's best interest to use Agent Pay and equivalents," Miebach said. Agent Pay is Mastercard's agentic commerce infrastructure that uses tokens to verify intent and other transactions specifications. Visa and American Express also have frameworks — called Visa Intelligent Commerce and Intent Intelligence, respectively — that use tokens to send information between the issuer, merchant and the consumer's AI agent. 

"We are not supporting solutions that take a one-time [virtual card number] as fronting a transaction," Miebach said. "That fundamentally breaks the transaction." 

Miebach said that Mastercard would support one-time virtual cards as a stopgap. "If a VCN is a processor decision that is a bridge to get ready for a fully tokenized transaction all the way through for a period of time, we're cognizant that this ecosystem needs to get there, no question about it, but that's not a long-term solution that we will support," he said. 

 Personal agentic assistants such as Muse and Instinct are helping ramp agentic transactions at "impressive weekly growth rates," Miebach said, but he stressed that it was still "early days" and the numbers were "not yet significant in the grand scheme. 

"We're now seeing the early stages of consumer adoption," he said, but noted that many merchants were still working to make their products discoverable by AI. 

"For this type of agentic commerce to function at scale, we need four things: trust in the payment, the agent, the ecosystem, and ubiquitous reach," Miebach said. "Even if everybody uses Agent Pay, that doesn't mean that every merchant is still discoverable."  

For the third quarter ended September 30, Mastercard posted a "solid 3Q beat," led by outperformance in payment network revenue and value-added service revenue, according to Keybanc analysts. Net revenue increased 14% from the prior year to $9.8 billion, with payment network revenue rising 11% to $5.8 billion and value-added service revenue increasing 19% to $4.1 billion. Cross-border volume grew 11%. 

"Increased payment volumes were driven by strong U.S. volumes, and intra-quarter trends show continued stability across spend metrics," Keefe Bruyette & Woods analyst Sanjay Sakhrani said in a research note.

Analysts at William Blair were also bullish on Mastercard following the company's earnings report. "Although macro has been a steady tailwind, we believe Mastercard can maintain consistent financial performance, owing to secular digital payments growth, share gains, pricing power, and leading [value-added services]," they said in a note.

data.title: Ex-Treasury Sec. Paulson urges US to tame national debt
data.description:
• Supporting data: The U.S. national debt is approximately $40.6 trillion, and rising.
  • Expert quote: "We are paying more to service our past than invest in our future." — Former U.S. Treasury secretary Hank Paulson

In 2008, then-Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson called America's largest financial institutions "too big to fail." Today, he says, the national debt is simply too big.

Paulson, who led the Treasury Department from 2006 to 2009, gave a speech Thursday calling for the United States to get its economic and political houses in order so it can more effectively lead the world. To do otherwise, he said, would risk disaster.

"No one knows how this new world will take shape. We are heading into uncharted waters," Paulson said at the Economic Club of New York. "But there is one thing I am certain of: American leadership is indispensable."

In a rapidly changing world, Paulson said, the U.S. faces three major challenges: taming its own dysfunctional politics, managing the risks and benefits of AI, and getting the "unsustainable" national debt under control.

"If not addressed, it will strangle our economy," Paulson said of the debt. "It will thwart our prosperity and destroy our national security, which is rooted in economic strength."

The U.S. national debt is currently about $40.6 trillion — about $119,000 per U.S. citizen — and rising. The interest on that debt is now more than $1 trillion per year.

"We are paying more to service our past than invest in our future," Paulson said. "Every

dollar that goes to interest is a dollar crowding out other necessary investments, like

research, infrastructure, defense or preparing workers for AI."

Paulson, who before running the Treasury was CEO of Goldman Sachs, predicted that sooner or later the national debt will cause a crisis. As out-of-control deficits erode the world's faith in the U.S. government, he warned, the country will eventually "hit the wall" when it loses creditworthiness or faces a run on U.S. Treasury securities.

"History has shown that crises are inevitable," he said. "So, we need to be prepared and

have an emergency contingency plan — a highly targeted, 'break-the-glass' policy on the shelf."

Paulson has plenty of experience with emergency measures. In 2008, when the global financial system was teetering on the brink of collapse, the Treasury secretary spearheaded a $700 billion bailout for American banks and other financial institutions, helping the George W. Bush administration push it through Congress.

The program faced severe criticism from both left-wing and right-wing detractors, but to this day Paulson believes it staved off a greater disaster.

"When you're dealing with a big, messy crisis, there's not an elegant solution," he said during a question-and-answer session. "We made our share of mistakes, but I'm able to look back and say we got the big things right."

Read more:

  • Fed will drop one interest rate vote next year; two in 2028
  • UMB says deal gives it access to wealth fleeing California
  • CFPB flunks cybersecurity audit amid staff cuts: OIG report
  • BofA adds Wisconsin to branch map, with more states to come

Paulson did not specify what a "break-the-glass" solution would look like in the event of a national debt crisis. But to avoid such a crisis in the first place, he recommended a few preventive measures to raise revenue and reduce spending.

"You could raise all the revenues we need to raise, without being a big drag on growth, if we just closed all the loopholes and preferences in the tax code," he said. "I also believe we can raise a lot of money painlessly through a value-added tax. We're one of the few countries in the world that doesn't have one."

Without referring directly to the current U.S. president, the Bush-era Treasury secretary also took issue with one Trump-era policy. 

"We need clear, durable rules so markets and trading partners know where the lines exist," Paulson said. "And unpredictable tariffs, especially on our allies, work against this. Reliability is an asset, and every time we surprise our partners, we draw it down."

data.title: When should RIAs hand clients to next-generation advisors?
data.description:
• Key insight: For firms that get it right, there are several strategies that ensure young advisors are ready to take on their own clients.
  • Expert quote:  "If [clients are] contacting you because they have an issue, and they want to know how to solve it, and they're bypassing me to go to that advisor, they're ready." Haleh "Holly" Moddasser.

Although he's been in the business for three decades, Anthony Skvarka, senior wealth advisor at Halbert Hargrove, remembers his early-career stage fright like it was yesterday. 

"I was petrified," he said. 

Skvarka, who eventually got over it through sheer repetition, credits the guidance of a good mentor. 

"I still work with that same guy," he said. "We are still aligned. He was my mentor, and he continues to be my mentor. However, we are now investment professionals together. We share some clients together, we have clients of our own, but we bounce things off each other. He still provides me with constructive criticism. That is so critical."

Firms continue to face a two-sided problem. Cerulli estimated more than 72% of early-career or "rookie" advisors left the profession in 2022. Meanwhile, senior talent grapples with sustainable succession planning, with nearly 110,000 advisors set to retire over the next decade. 

Putting young talent into positions they aren't fully equipped for presents as much potential for fallout as refusing to promote and develop them. This makes finding a firmwide sweet spotamong juniors, longstanding clients and older advisors key. 

It also makes knowing the signs that a junior advisor is in the right place all the more important. 

They know how to inherit business rather than hunt for it

The first step toward ensuring an advisor will make the senior ranks is simply ensuring that they're a good fit for the firm. 

Haleh "Holly" Moddasser is a managing director and senior wealth advisor at Hightower Signature Wealth who has worked to hire and develop a next-generation talent team for roughly a decade. 

At her firm, rather than overwhelm next-gen advisors with the need to produce revenue, "we literally hired them to be able to inherit a book from [the first generation]," she said. 

To keep the strategy intact, the firm hired people who were "mutually aligned, fit our firm culture, right age, stage and credentials," she said. "And then we had them start joining us in meetings with our longtime clients."

At Halbert Hargrove, younger talent readiness begins at the hiring and culture levels. Skvarka said the firm hires for passion and fit, "because we don't want turnover." 

In fact, "we don't have a lot of turnover." The firm takes its time hiring and "they don't all [start out wanting] to be an advisor," he said. "They may turn into that or they may turn into something else."

They know and develop their expertise from day one

Moddasser sets up team meetings by repositioning herself as a big-picture strategist and relationship manager and then introducing the next-gen team members as experts. For instance, if a client needs the year's required minimum distribution, the planner is their point person. For investment strategy, the team leans on the portfolio advisor. 

"My thought is that the client gets the best experience when you're not asking each individual advisor to be all things to that client," she said. 

She puts together what she calls a "diamond team" that combines a planner, investment specialist and the first-generation team member, ensuring every client is used to two or three people handling the relationship.

"I became the relationship manager and basically the one who is selling work and immediately introduced them as part of the team that is actually the nuts and bolts of the business," she said. After time went by, "I actually leveraged their highest and best use. I didn't throw them in there and say, 'I need you to pound the pavement and bring in some business.'" 

They earn the lead one piece at a time

At Modera, according to Jeanne Bernardin, principal and wealth manager, before a next-generation advisor is promoted to work with clients, certain fundamentals need to be in place. Prior to client meetings, the team has its prep meetings where junior team members are expected to explain topics clearly and follow through. 

"As we're doing meeting prep," she said, junior team members "go through with me how they would present this to a client," which she considers a progressive approach for leading client meetings.

In those prep sessions, "we are talking about who will lead different parts of the meeting, so this is where it comes to a progression [where they're] involved in leading pieces of the meeting once they've shown competency, reliability and discipline," she said. 

Clients seek them out individually

A 25-year-old looking to appeal to a 60-year-old prospect during a pitch is a recipe for trouble, according to Moddasser. That's why she doesn't send juniors out to pitch.

But over time and with enough exposure to one another, relationships can and do evolve. 

At Modera, the final step is making sure the young advisor has a more personalized connection with the client. 

"They understand what their needs are, what drives their decisions and can really connect with the client," said Bernardin. "You see that trust developed, the client's going to them more frequently as the first point of contact." 

A client reaching out about an appointment or moving money from one account to another is "not confidence," according to Moddasser. "If they're contacting you because they have an issue, and they want to know how to solve it, and they're bypassing me to go to that advisor, they're ready," she said. 

Skvarka agreed that the personalized relationship is a cornerstone signal, but cautioned that it takes time to get to that level. 

"Success just doesn't naturally come overnight," he said. "They have to be willing to commit to a certain level of understanding that they're just not going to roll in and take over somebody's book of business."

According to Moddasser, first-generation advisors who've spent decades in the seat may resist relinquishing the controls. The veterans need to be willing to make this mental transition for it to work. 

"You can take great satisfaction in watching them become a star as opposed to you always having to be the star," she said. 

Moddasser saw this firsthand when an eye injury left her unable to read or look at a Zoom screen. Her team initially panicked, but she told them they were ready, "and they were."

"You have to believe in them," she said. "Not falsely believe in them, but they've demonstrated, they've done, they've been a star."

Although bittersweet, "it's like launching kids," she said. "You don't want them to leave you, but they have to spread their wings and go … that's part of your job, to let them go."

data.title: Happen Bank ties 26% credit growth to home improvement loans
data.description:
Key insight: Happen Bank, the entity formerly known as LendingClub, reported strong results its first quarter under its new name.

Expert quote: "We are four months into the rebrand [and] searches for Happen Bank are already more than two times those for LendingClub." —Scott Sanborn, CEO, Happen Bank

Happen Bank, formerly known as LendingClub before completing a rebrand earlier this year, completed its first quarter under its new name.

"This was our first full quarter operating as Happen Bank, and the early response has been terrific," CEO Scott Sanborn said during the company's after-market earnings call on Wednesday. "We are four months into the rebrand [and] searches for Happen Bank are already more than two times those for LendingClub."

Happen Bank's earnings hit multiple records this quarter, according to the company. Pre-tax income rose 34% year-over-year to $76.8 million and diluted earnings per share (EPS) increased 35% year-over-year to $0.50, matching last quarter's EPS results. The company raised its full-year EPS outlook to between $1.87 and $1.92 from the previous expected range of $1.80 to $1.90.

Part of that income line was from another sequential adjustment to the company's provision for credit losses. This quarter, the provision line was reported as a benefit of approximately $16 million for the company, continuing a trend of positive provision adjustments that Happen Bank started earlier in the year.

"We expect credit performance to remain solid in the fourth quarter, and we anticipate a further provision benefit of $5 million to $10 million," Happen Bank Chief Financial Officer Andrew LaBenne said in the earnings call.

Deposits grew by 22% year-over-year to $11.5 billion and loan originations climbed 26% to $3.34 billion, driven by personal loans and the company's entry into the home improvement market. Sanborn told investors that the response to the company's new home improvement loan products has been "really strong."

"Customers have so much equity in their homes and are sort of stuck, given that the vast majority of mortgages are now below six when rates for new mortgages are in the sevens," Sanborn said. "People are deciding, 'I am staying put, so I might as well make this place what I want it to be.' We can help with affordable payments and financing."

Happen Bank is also on track to launch a home equity line of credit (HELOC) offering in the second half of next year, Sanborn said. "Consumers are tapping roughly $21 trillion in home equity to consolidate debt and make home improvements, two areas where we already have experience," he said.

Happen Bank's lending products were partially affected by the Federal Reserve's interest rate hike earlier this year. Higher rates led to about $20 million of markdowns in the third quarter due to higher funding costs. 

According to the bank, however, the markdowns were offset by the bank's hedging program, which was increased from $1.5 billion to $2.5 billion to manage rate risk. The hedges led to a $15 million gain.  LaBenne said in the earnings call. "We plan to expand our hedging program as we grow to manage our interest rate risk profile. Our goal is to protect revenue generated by the balance sheet through interest rate cycles within prescribed limits."

A Citizens analyst research note called the bank's hedging activities "a positive dynamic." 

"We believe that the company's funding model is more complex and resilient versus competitors, primarily fintechs," the note read. "Rate hikes are providing Happen with a competitive advantage as fintech competitors struggle to re-price personal loans. With at least one more rate hike expected by the Street this year, we see this margin pressure on near-prime fintech competitors continuing."

Happen Bank's rebrand, undergone partially to include "bank" in the company's name, concluded a multi-year process which began when it received an OCC bank charter through buying Radius Bancorp and its subsidiary, Radius Bank, for $185 million back in 2020. The company officially became a bank in February 2021 once the acquisition was complete.

Sanborn described Happen's current competitive position as a "six-year head start" in comparison to other fintechs applying for bank charters over the past 18 months.

"We see all of the fintechs pursuing bank charters as validating the idea that we pursued six years ago," Sanborn said. "When we became a bank, we had to be operationally ready out of the gate. With the conditional approvals today, most of these banks are not yet operating as banks. They should be hitting the market throughout the course of next year, [and] we feel very ready to compete."

Sanborn also told investors that Happen Bank is preparing to work with external AI agents in the near future, as other large banks are blocking agents from accessing customer accounts or rewriting their terms and conditions to place liability for agent activity on the consumer.

"AI agents are coming to banking," he said. "We believe that we stand to benefit, and we plan to be ready. When consumer trust, permission and liability issues are sufficiently resolved, that value proposition will remain and we are making the investments now to be both highly visible and responsibly accessible to agents when the time comes."

data.title: Freddie Mac's loan acquisitions top Fannie's as rates rise
data.description:
• Key Insight: See why Freddie Mac's new loan acquisitions moved ahead of Fannie Mae's in the third quarter.
  • What's at Stake: Competition between Fannie and Freddie could make them more willing to open up the credit box for lenders who sell loans to them.

A profitable Freddie Mac regained its lead over larger competitor Fannie Mae in single-family loan acquisitions during the third quarter as higher rates intensified competition between them.
Freddie, which is the smaller of the two government-sponsored enterprises when it comes to its outstanding portfolio size, reported Thursday that it acquired $98 billion in home mortgages during the fiscal period. Fannie Mae, in comparison, purchased $88 billion in single-family loans.

These and other numbers in their recent earnings raises the question of what Freddie is doing to capture more loan acquisitions and whether it's opening up the credit box to do it.

The latest underwriting indicators in earnings show Freddie's credit score and loan-to-value ratio tolerances are slightly higher, but the growth in credit reserves and some elevated delinquency measures at both GSEs suggests both will be cautious about the size of their credit boxes.

"We are growing our financial strength, applying disciplined decision-making and risk management, and continuing to invest in the capabilities that can make the housing system work better," Freddie Mac Chief Financial Officer Jim Whitlinger said in the GSE's earnings call.

What underwriting indicators show

Whitlinger reported that Freddie's weighted average current loan-to-value ratio was 54% and the equivalent credit score was 755 in the company's third-quarter earnings call. Fannie's equivalent credit score number was 753 and its mark-to-market loan-to-value ratio was 51%.

Current or mark-to-market LTVs on the outstanding portfolios account for property value changes and paydowns on loans over time. Weighted averages for original LTVs are generally higher and have averaged more around 78%, according to Fannie.

The underwriting metrics for new acquisitions are a subset of the broader portfolio numbers. Whitlinger and others have indicated there may be more caution in that part of the market because slight increases in certain delinquency buckets have been driven by newer vintages.

"The year-over-year increase was primarily driven by higher serious delinquency rates for loans originated during 2022 through 2024," Whitlinger said during the call.

Both Fannie and Freddie have seen some delinquencies inch up in both their single- and multifamily book, calling for broader risk management.

With risk growing, Freddie had to manage a larger-than anticipated shift from a $900 million benefit for credit losses to a $800 million reserve during the quarter, analysts at BTIG noted. Fannie also recorded a shift from a benefit for credit losses to a reserve in the period.

All this suggests that for the time being, Freddie and Fannie are keeping an eye on credit, which may limit how much leeway in underwriting they want to use to compete.

But they still want to offer some additional support to help consumers afford homes to the extent their delinquency rates and overall financials allow. While some types of arrears are rising, the single-family serious delinquency rate is still historically low at less than 1% at both GSEs.

"Financial strength matters because of what it enables us to do," Whitlinger said. "It gives us greater capacity to provide liquidity throughout the economic cycle, support sustainable homeownership and help make housing finance more efficient and affordable."

Examples include a lender option that both GSEs now offer to use the modernized VantageScore 4.0 credit metric for loan pricing, which some mortgage companies have said helped them get certain borrowers approved. This was used for 6% of the loans Fredddie bought in the third quarter, Whitlinger said.

Other key financial metrics to watch

The GSEs so far have shown that they are financially strong from a net income perspective and have sustained the long run of profitability that followed their 2008 move into conservatorship.

So long as that financial strength persists, they might do more to expand some underwriting selectively with offsetting, more conservative adjustments in other areas in line with the trend seen in the condo market.

Freddie reported that quarterly net income rose by around 17% on the year to $3.2 billion, and Fannie announced a day earlier that its strongest net revenues since 2023 drove an 8% increase during the same period to $4.2 billion.

The smaller GSE's $3.2 billion in growth for the quarter also brought its total net worth to $81 billion, helping to close a regulatory capital gap that's also essential to their financial soundness and an eventual conservatorship exit. Fannie also reported improvement in this area.

"Excluding buffers, our capital shortfall was $98 billion at the end of third quarter 2026, largely because the $73 billion of senior preferred stock does not qualify," Whitlinger said in a reminder that an exit would need to address this, a key point prominent GSE investors have emphasized.

Adjusted for the SPS, this means capital is around $21 billion below its statutory minimum level, Keefe, Bruyette & Woods analysts noted in a report on Freddie's earnings.

"FMCC's capital remains subordinate to the government's senior preferred shares and liquidation preference, so any privatization would have to include either forgiveness or conversion," the KBW analysts wrote.

Both Freddie and Fannie's shares were trading higher on the day at press time on Thursday, with the former's stock up by a little over 12% at $4.09 per share and latter's around 8% at $4.48.

data.title: Amex recruits its next chief risk officer from U.S. Bancorp
data.description:
• Key insight: Jodi Richard, who has been chief risk officer at U.S. Bancorp for the past eight years, is set to join American Express in January. 
  • What's at stake: Richard will oversee Amex's global risk organization as the payments company addresses alleged anti-money-laundering deficiencies.

American Express has recruited one of U.S. Bancorp's most senior executives to become its new chief risk officer, part of a broader management shuffle at the payments company.

Jodi Richard, who has served for eight years as chief risk officer at Minneapolis-based U.S. Bancorp, will join Amex in January. She will report to CEO Stephen Squeri, who announced the hiring Thursday in a memo to Amex employees. Richard will be based in New York and join Amex's management committee.

One of American Banker's Most Powerful Women in Banking for the past several years, Richard will succeed Doug Tabish. Tabish will become Amex's president of enterprise shared services upon the retirement of Denise Pickett in February 2027.

Amex announced Pickett's retirement plans and Tabish's new role in a Wednesday memo, saying that Tabish will also report to Squeri.

As Amex's chief risk officer, Richard will lead its global risk organization and "help ensure" that it continues to "balance innovation, growth and disciplined risk management" as it pursues its strategy, Squeri said in Thursday's memo. He called Richard "an accomplished risk executive" and noted that earlier in her career, she worked as a national bank examiner for the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.

Prior to joining U.S. Bank's parent company in 2014, Richard was the head of operational risk and internal control at HSBC North America.

"Throughout her career in banking, Jodi has demonstrated that risk management should be an effective partner to the business, and that while the need to innovate and grow is important, what is even more critical is taking the right risks responsibly," Squeri wrote. "This is imperative to protecting our customers and our company while enabling the business to move forward."

Amex's hiring of Richard comes as the company addresses certain alleged deficiencies in its financial crimes risk-management program. Earlier this month, the OCC and the Federal Reserve issued cease-and-desist orders against the company's banking arm and ordered it to improve its anti-money-laundering compliance program. The OCC fined Amex $350 million in connection with the alleged deficiencies.

In its consent order, the OCC alleged that Amex "experienced systemic breakdowns in its suspicious activity monitoring and reporting processes." It said those breakdowns resulted in the company failing to report about $13 billion of suspected trade-based money laundering between 2014 and 2025.

In response to the regulatory orders, Squeri said that Amex "takes its responsibility to combat financial crimes seriously" and that it is "fully committed" to addressing regulators' concerns. He also said the company had made "substantial investments" in areas such as people, technology, governance and training in order to better identify and respond to financial-crime risks.

Richard's last day at the $703 billion-asset U.S. Bancorp will be this Friday, U.S. Bancorp CEO Gunjan Kedia told employees in a memo. Kedia added that Richard "has led a talented organization of professionals who have worked to build true risk management excellence at the company."

Read more:

  • Fed will drop one interest rate vote next year; two in 2028
