  • UMB says deal gives it access to wealth fleeing California
  • CFPB flunks cybersecurity audit amid staff cuts: OIG report
  • BofA adds Wisconsin to branch map, with more states to come

Richard was promoted to chief risk officer in 2018, a challenging time for U.S. Bancorp. In February of that year, the bank admitted to looking the other way regarding certain suspicious accounts and concealing from its regulator key information regarding its efforts to combat money laundering.

The bank was charged with two felony violations and ultimately entered into a deferred prosecution agreement with the U.S. Attorney's Office in the Southern District of New York. U.S. Bancorp also agreed to pay $613 million in penalties.

In early 2025, U.S. Bancorp awarded Richard a one-time retention award valued at $3 million, in the form of restricted stock units. The award was based on Richard's "critical role within the company in the current operating environment, the strength of the company's risk management program, and Ms. Richard's strong performance," the bank said in its most recent proxy statement.

Fifty percent of the retention award was scheduled to vest on each of the third and fourth anniversary of the grant date, the proxy statement said.

U.S. Bancorp said Thursday that Troy Remington, its chief credit officer, will serve as interim chief risk officer while the bank begins a search for Richard's permanent successor.

Kedia expressed confidence that U.S. Bancorp will be able to appoint a new chief risk officer quickly.

data.title: ICE execs brush off spinoff talk amid mortgage challenges
data.description:
Intercontinental Exchange executives highlighted lending technology wins and the ongoing development of artificial intelligence infrastructure, but they also faced questions about the wisdom of mortgage investments over the past decade and even a possible spinoff. 

In its third-quarter earnings call, leaders addressed the performance and future prospects of ICE Mortgage Technology amid what is expected to be the most challenging lending environment in years. 

"Part of building an all-weather company is having a company that will do well when interest rates are rising and when interest rates are falling," said ICE CEO Jeff Sprecher during the call. 

The financial technology giant, which also owns market exchanges and fixed income and data services businesses, has made headline acquisitions to grow the other parts of the company this year. Executives noted that some of its past investments, whose values were criticized at the time, are now drivers of growth. 

The Atlanta-based enterprise took ownership of Ellie Mae and its Encompass loan-origination system in 2020 and followed up with an acquisition of the Black Knight servicing platform three years later.

The comments highlight heightened challenges that have emerged in 2026, forcing many companies to alter their strategies this year. 

"That being said, we're not married to anything. We're here as stewards of capital," Sprecher added, alluding to any possible future spinoff of segments. "If some of the parts don't work, then we'll find different parts."

Despite the challenging macro environment posed by current mortgage rates and housing costs, company leaders also pointed out that the home finance unit was performing well under pressure after its second consecutive profitable quarter.

ICE announces AI upgrades

As it focuses on artificial intelligence advancements on its origination and mortgage-servicing platforms, ICE Mortgage Technology also announced changes its customers could expect to see during the call, including enhanced AI access to its infrastructure.

"Starting this quarter, customers will be able to deploy their own agents connecting to either Encompass or MSP through a model context protocol in a fully auditable way," said Intercontinental Exchange President Ben Jackson, who also serves as chair of ICE Mortgage Technology. 

"Several of our clients are already engaging with us on this," he added, noting their ability to work with the wealth of data and permissions already available on ICE's systems. 

Jackson's comments came as the mortgage unit sees rising competition from a number of growing technology firms celebrating their recent additions of new customers. Competitors have frequently highlighted how AI serves as the foundation of their tools compared to older legacy systems. 

In the third quarter, though, ICE Mortgage Technology was able to boast of its own deals, Jackson pointed out. They included the company's broadening relationship with Wells Fargo Bank after the banking giant agreed to move its home-equity portfolio to MSP.

The servicing platform has added five new clients in 2026, the company said. 

ICE Mortgage Technology profits in the third quarter

Between July and September, the mortgage business at Intercontinental Exchange delivered operating income of $13 million to finish in the black, although profits shrank from both the prior quarter and year. Income decreased 71% from second-quarter's $45 million and 41% from $22 million over the same three months in 2025.

The number came off of revenue of $549 million, which was a 1.4% decrease from the previous three-month total of $557 million. It rose 4% on a year-over-year basis from $528 million. 

Its MSP servicing software, which it acquired from Black Knight in 2023, raked in $229 million, a lift when compared to $226 million and $216 million three and 12 months earlier.

Meanwhile, its origination-technology business took in $189 million, down from $197 million in the second quarter but inching up from $188 million a year ago. 

While looming challenges — including expected consolidation of the mortgage industry and rates remaining above 7% into 2027 — might pose threats to the recurring revenue that comes from existing-client renewals, ICE expressed confidence for the unit's expansion.

"We can continue to grow that business as we have been over the last couple of years in what's been a challenging macro," said ICE Chief Financial Officer Warren Gardiner. "The important thing for that is we continue to invest in the business."

On an adjusted pro forma basis, which calculates earnings by folding in hypothetical Black Knight financials, operating income finished at $219 million, which was down from $239 million and $224 million on a quarterly and yearly basis.  

"This quarter also marks three years since we closed our acquisition of Black Knight, and the integration continues to deliver ahead of plan," Gardiner said. "We now expect to exit 2026 with approximately $270 million of annualized expense synergies. This compares to an original 5-year target of $200 million when we announced the transaction."

data.title: Watch spreads, not the Fed, for mortgage rate shifts
data.description:
• Expert Quote: "It's been a while since the Fed was the main character in the mortgage rates narrative." — Kate Wood, Lending Expert, NerdWallet
  • Supporting Data: A 225 basis point spread currently separating Treasurys and mortgages. 

 Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review.   

Investors' concerns over whether artificial intelligence companies will be able to handle their debt loads helped to push the 10-year Treasury yield back under the 5% floor this past week.

This reduction helped the average for the 30-year fixed rate mortgage fall by 8 basis points for a second consecutive week, Freddie Mac said.

But the 10-year Treasury still remains close to 5%, making mortgage industry observers wary about its effect on long-term rates, even with the Federal Open Market Committee's decision to stand pat on Wednesday.

"We often see more movement from mortgage rates in anticipation of Federal Reserve meetings than we do once the decisions are actually announced, and with this widely expected pause we didn't even see that," said Kate Wood, NerdWallet's lending expert. "It's been a while since the Fed was the main character in the mortgage rates narrative."

If anything, it is the market reaction to what is happening with the AI companies, putting money into Treasurys even with higher inflation, that has been driving mortgage rates lower, Wood said.

Mortgage rates this week

The 30-year FRM averaged 7.24% for Oct. 29, the Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey reported. This is down from last week's 7.32%. However, a year ago, this product averaged 6.17% or 108 basis points lower than the current rate.

For this week, the 15-year FRM averaged 6.6%, also a decline of 8 basis points from the Oct. 22 PMMS. For the same week in 2025 it averaged 5.41%.

"The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage declined again this week, reaching its lowest level this month and modestly boosting purchasing power for prospective buyers," said Sam Khater, Freddie Mac's chief economist, in a press release.

Lender Price data posted on the National Mortgage News website on Thursday morning had the 30-year FRM at 7.55%, more than 20 basis points lower than a week ago, reflecting the changed Treasury environment.

The 10-year was 4.98% as of 11 a.m. Last Thursday, the 10-year closed at 4.95% after ending the previous day at 5.15%.

Still, most observers are holding to their views for rates to stay above 7% for at least the next two months, if not beyond.

How originators viewed the FOMC announcement

"Higher for longer isn't a forecast anymore, it's the environment," said Hector Amendola, the president of SimplyPMG. "I don't know where rates go and I won't pretend to."

The supply of homes for sale is better now than a year ago and based on what he is seeing in his own pipeline, sellers are more willing to make concessions.

"Buyers doing well right now stopped watching the announcement and started working on the long game and focusing on what they qualify for today," Amendola said.

In a statement issued after the Fed decision but before this morning's Personal Consumption Expenditures index release, Melissa Cohn, regional vice president at William Raveis Mortgage said the FOMC is "very likely" to hike at its December meeting if inflation hasn't improved.

"We can hope that the markets remain stable and last week's rate improvements hold," Cohn continued. "Where mortgage rates go next will largely depend on oil prices and the war in Iran."

In the opinion of mortgage and structured credit investment strategy company Dundon E1, the most important development for mortgage rates is the guidance the FOMC issued with the decision, said Victor Baev, its chief investment officer, on Wednesday.

"Two members of the committee voted in favor of another increase, and the statement kept the possibility of a further hike at the December meeting on the table," Baev said. "That tells the bond market that short-term rates are likely to remain at or above current levels for an extended period."

This likelihood is already priced into the 10-year, one of the mechanisms used to set mortgage rates, he said. Mostly agreeing with Cohn, Baev said inflation is what home buyers have to look at, not what the Fed does at any individual meeting. 

"The 30-year fixed rate has risen roughly 70 basis points since late August as the market adjusted to the September increase, and last week's reading represented the first weekly decline in two months," Baev noted. "Until the inflation numbers show clearer progress toward the Fed's 2% target, we would expect the weekly survey to remain in the low 7% range."

From Wood's perspective, "If it looks like December won't be the last, that could change the outlook on inflation. But whether that puts upward pressure on mortgage rates may depend on which investors fear more: Inflation eroding the value of bonds or inflation making it less likely AI investments will pay off."

Just shy of 80% of the traders on CME FedWatch are expecting a 25 basis point hike at the December meeting.

The current Treasury-to-mortgage spread is 225 basis points, the widest in a year and above the historical norm of 150 basis points to 200 basis points. If the spreads do return to their normal levels, "mortgage rates could decline even while the Federal Reserve holds its policy rate steady, and as investors in these markets, that is the dynamic we are watching most closely," Baev said.

The tradeoff between rates and rising home prices

Zillow Home Loans' current forecast is for the 30-year to remain above 7% this year, but to be at 6.5% or higher in 2027, said Kara Ng, senior economist.

"For a buyer who has decided to purchase a home, but is questioning when, here is the tradeoff," Ng said. "Borrowing costs are expected to ease, but only slightly. Home values, meanwhile, are expected to rise modestly nationwide, offsetting some of the savings from lower rates."

Her advice: buy now, as waiting a year would only reduce the monthly mortgage payment by $26.

If anything, the Mortgage Bankers Association's Purchase Applications Payment Index rose $53 in September from August to $2,215.

"Despite a slight decline in the median loan amount, higher mortgage rates drove monthly payments upward, with affordability deteriorating in 39 states" said Edward Seiler, MBA's associate vice president of housing economics and executive director of the Research Institute for Housing America. "Compared to a year ago, mortgage payments are up more than 7%, outpacing earnings growth and adding to the affordability challenges facing prospective homebuyers."

The MBA does not expect any significant mortgage rate relief over its housing forecast timeline, said Mike Fratantoni, chief economist.

"Mortgage rates now at three-year highs are causing a sharp slowdown in home sales, mortgage originations, and in commercial real estate markets," Fratantoni said. "Although the Fed did not increase short-term rates, the market has already priced in at least another couple of hikes over the near term, in line with MBA's forecast."

No October Fed increase as 'a dangerous gamble' for mortgages

The Fed decision to hold is a "dangerous gamble," for both the U.S. economy and mortgages, said Nigel Green, CEO of the deVere Group, in his commentary.

He pointed to the Fed's slow reaction to inflation in 2021, not moving until March 2022.

"The Fed was asleep at the wheel, and families paid for it at the checkout, at the pump and on their mortgages," said Green. Those same warnings signs are flashing again, noting the 10-year's current status, plus the 7.4% 30-year FRM Freddie Mac reported two weeks ago.

"If the Fed won't tighten, bond investors will do it for them, and they're far less gentle," he said.

The market expects a tighter FOMC monetary policy in the future, "propping up mortgage rates above 7% for the near term," said Eric Orenstein, Fitch Ratings senior director. "We expect the smaller origination market in 2027 to limit earnings upside for mortgage companies."

data.title: Hassett sees Fed acting if October inflation data come in high
data.description:
(Bloomberg) -- White House National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett hinted that he expected the Federal Reserve would raise interest rates if inflation figures for this month are elevated.

"If October comes out really high, then I think the Fed would probably appropriately act," Hassett said in a Bloomberg Television interview Thursday. After the month's consumer price index and so-called PCE price gauge are out, "at that point, I think it would be clear what the Fed should do," he said.

Hassett was speaking shortly after the latest PCE inflation report showed that core price gains, which exclude food and energy, clocked a 3.1% year-on-year pace for September. Overall PCE inflation ran at 3.6% last month, well over the Fed's 2% target. He said that if October prices slow, that would suggest September was just a "blip."

On Wednesday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was asked if he'd view any future Fed rate increase as a policy mistake. He responded on CNBC, "that's not necessarily so," and cited strong economic growth.

Hassett also indicated he had little issue with the two dissenting votes in favor of raising interest rates on the policymaking Federal Open Market Committee on Wednesday. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh "has done a good job of allowing normal dissent and driving a consensus," he said.

"His committee has made a decision that looks very data-driven to us, and so I don't have a concern about the committee right now," Hassett said.

Fed Governor Lisa Cook and Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Beth Hammack voted in favor of raising rates this week. Cook is the target of a panel set up by the White House to investigate mortgage-fraud allegations the administration has levied against her. Hassett is one of the three panel members, and declined to comment on the deliberations. He did say that "people can dissent if they want, it's a completely fair process."

More stories like this are available on bloomberg.com

data.title: Fannie Mae logs title, appraisal savings; net revenues soar
data.description:
• Key Insight: Why Fannie Mae came out ahead in earnings despite mixed impacts from higher rates, and has new reason to press forward with title alternatives.
  • Supporting Data: Fannie found borrowers' collective savings from appraisal and title alternatives so far this year have been over $100 million.
    Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review.

Fannie Mae reported its highest net revenues since 2023 and revealed significant mission-related borrower savings from title and appraisal alternative initiatives in the third quarter, when it contended with mixed impacts from higher rates but was still able to hold costs for lenders relatively low.
Consumer savings from the title and appraisal waiver programs show these alternatives got enough use to drive a 7-figure reduction in origination expenses. They also reinforce a recent executive order backing both and transitioning Fannie's title alternative pilot to a national program with monitoring.

"Our efforts to provide appraisal and title insurance alternatives helped borrowers save an estimated $141 million in closing costs so far this year," Peter Akwaboah, acting CEO and chief operating officer at Fannie Mae said during the government-related loan buyer's earnings call.

Fannie was able to support such housing affordability initiatives with $4.2 billion in net income, representing a 5% rise from the previous quarter and an 8% increase from a year ago, even though higher rates diminished the industry originations it buys.

The government-sponsored enterprise's executives explained why during its earnings call.

Why fewer acquisitions didn't hurt revenue

"Changes in interest rates affect various aspects of our financial results. For example, in single-family, while higher rates tend to reduce acquisition volumes, they also slow prepayments and book runoff, helping to preserve guaranty revenues," Chief Financial Officer Chryssa Halley noted during the company's call.

Fannie's core guaranty business fueled 79% of its $7.7 billion in total net revenues, which drove the government-sponsored enterprise's earnings gain.

Single-family loan acquisition volumes did fall by roughly 21% from the previous quarter and around 11% from a year earlier to $88 billion in line with some industry declines, but with refinancing representing only $18 billion of that total, prepayments for Fannie were reduced.

Refi activity in the dominant single-family business matched year-ago levels but was down nearly 53% from the previous quarter. 

In addition to affecting prepayments and loan volume in the quarter, this may have another impact, according to Halley.

"From an allowance perspective, slow prepayments extend the expected life of our loans, which combined with higher mortgage costs for certain borrowers can increase our expected credit losses," she said.

Serious and 60-day delinquencies in the single-family sector remained historically low but have been drifting generally higher in the past year, ending at 62 and 92 basis points, respectively, in the third quarter. They were both nearly 20 basis points lower than a year earlier.

Sixty-day delinquencies were 7 basis points lower the previous quarter. Serious delinquencies were 4 basis points lower compared to the same period. Thirty-day delinquencies matched the previous quarter's 1.09%, but were below the 1% level reported a year earlier.

Fannie recorded a total single- and multifamily allowance for credit losses of $1.1 billion, offset by other developments that included $630 million in fair value gains. The GSE also reported $94 million in investment gains. It additionally took $1 billion in net unrealized losses in its available-for-sale portfolio.

Efficiency initiatives and regulatory capital

Fannie also engaged in further efficiency initiatives during the quarter that Halley said offset some personnel costs for increased salaries, benefits and a $28 million severance expense. Expenditures on occupancy and technology were $52 million lower than the previous quarter.

Fannie reported a total adjusted capital deficit of $11 billion for the quarter, down from $14 billion in the previous three-month period. Its illustrative return on average required tier 1 capital was 11.1% in the quarter, up from 10.8%. 

"Despite volatility across aspects of our financial results, we increased net income both quarter over quarter and year over year, growing net worth to more than $119 billion while reducing our regulatory capital deficit," Halley said.

data.title: Why the way advisors talk about Social Security changes claiming plans
data.description:
• Forward look: Even as the Claiming Age Clarity Act awaits enactment to establish "minimum," "standard," and "maximum" benefit labels, wealth managers will still need to clearly explain options to their clients.
  • Expert quote: "A problem that advisors face is that the client already comes in with a preconceived idea that they're going to claim at age whatever-that-is, and you got to either say, 'Yes, that's a good idea,' or most of the time, 'No, that's probably too early. Have you thought about X, Y and Z?'" — Eric Ludwig, American College of Financial Services

Advisors will likely still need to help clients understand the ramifications of various Social Security claiming ages despite legislation aimed at clarifying terminology.

H.R. 5284, called the Claiming Age Clarity Act, passed the Senate on Sept. 29 after passing the House in December 2025, and it is related to the findings of an Oct. 1 research paper about how advisors should talk to clients about when to claim their benefits.

This legislation, which awaits President Donald Trump's signature, would change the Social Security Administration's terminology from the "early eligibility age" of 62 to "minimum monthly benefit age." The "full retirement age" and "normal retirement age" of 65 to 67 (depending on birth year) would change to "standard monthly benefit age." Lastly, the SSA would be required to refer to the "maximum monthly benefit age" of 70 instead of referring to a "delayed retirement credit."

But researchers at the American College of Financial Services found no difference in individuals' choices based on terminology alone. Instead, they said advisors should find out what clients' preconceived ideas are about Social Security and work from there to help them understand.

"A problem that advisors face is that the client already comes in with a preconceived idea that they're going to claim at age whatever-that-is, and you got to either say, 'Yes, that's a good idea,' or most of the time, 'No, that's probably too early. Have you thought about X, Y and Z?'" said Eric Ludwig, director of the Center for Retirement Income and an associate professor of retirement income at the American College of Financial Services.

The researchers — Ludwig and his co-author, Loren Flood, director of curriculum and an assistant professor at the American College of Financial Services — found that claiming decisions were influenced by which boundaries clients already knew about.

The study, which was a survey-based experiment with 1,603 respondents younger than 60 years old, found that only 12.7% of respondents knew both the minimum and maximum ages of 62 and 70, while 64.1% knew neither age. The percentage that knew about age 62 — 14.5% — was larger than the percentage who knew about age 70, which was 8.7%.

If respondents only knew the earliest possible age to claim benefits, they would plan to claim 0.86 years earlier, whereas if they only knew about the latest age, they would intend to claim 0.62 years later.

"Advisors should identify the client's existing anchors before building the recommendation," Ludwig said in an email. "There also appears to be a basic misunderstanding that retirement age and Social Security claiming age have to be the same."

Different methods of analysis

Although some might suspect retirees opt to claim Social Security earlier out of concern about the trust fund becoming depleted, the study found it wasn't a statistically significant driver of claiming age, Ludwig said.

"That concern deserves to be acknowledged, then answered with facts, such as what the projected shortfall would and wouldn't mean for their benefit," Flood added. "When offered as education rather than correction, the client can weigh the evidence for themselves. It also builds trust in the client-advisor relationship."

Showing clients dollar amounts rather than only percentages or ages is also helpful, said Flood.

The break-even age is another factor the researchers considered. Claiming benefits at an older age means receiving larger payments, but claiming benefits earlier means starting to receive payments sooner, even if those payments are smaller. There is a break-even point, often between ages 78 and 81. But the researchers discouraged advisors from focusing on that break-even analysis.

"The break-even-oriented messages did not produce later claiming intentions, while the age-based explanations did," Ludwig said. "Break-even framing can also make Social Security feel more like an investment decision with risk-and-reward tradeoffs [rather] than a source of lifetime income protection."

Claiming-age decisions are about more than math

In practice, it is rare for clients to know just one end of the claiming range, though perhaps they know about age 62 from other people in their lives, according to Samuel Diarbakerly, the founder and CEO of Boston-based wealth management firm Generation Capital Advisors.

He said it is more common for clients to lack understanding of how the benefit works, adding that even with all the education advisors bring, no one can account for all variables.

"We don't know how long they'll live, and we don't know what tax rates will be in the future," Diarbakerly told Financial Planning in a statement. "That's why we don't treat claiming as a bet on a break-even age. We treat it as a decision about protecting lifetime income under uncertainty."

Social Security claiming decisions and advisors' approaches to talking about them have as much or more to do with behavior and psychology than they have to do with calculating when might be the optimal time to claim benefits based on financial circumstances and life expectancy probabilities.

"It's of critical importance … how advisors present that information, in a manner that's more relatable from a behavioral-finance side than just bringing the math," said Robert J. Patterson, CEO of San Diego-based RIA  RJ Patterson Group.

For instance, younger individuals tend to think differently about when to claim Social Security than older individuals who are closer to actually claiming, Patterson said.

"It's very dependent on the individual's current mental state, situation [and] cash-flow needs," he said.
